etymologies.etymologyHTML: From earlier English ternado, attested since the 1550s as a nautical term for a windy thunderstorm. From Spanish tronada (“thunderstorm”), from tronar (“to thunder”), from Latin tonō (“to thunder”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). The o and r were reversed in English (metathesis) under influence of Spanish tornar (“to twist, to turn”), from Latin tornō (“to turn”).

definitions.definition: (meteorology) A violent wind in the form of a mobile, rapidly rotating, funnel cloud that has contacted the ground.

quote.citation: 2013 March, Frank Fish, George Lauder, “Not Just Going with the Flow”, in American Scientist‎[1], volume 101, number 2, archived from the original on 1 May 2013, page 114:
quote.text: An extreme version of vorticity is a vortex. The vortex is a spinning, cyclonic mass of fluid, which can be observed in the rotation of water going down a drain, as well as in smoke rings, tornados and hurricanes.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To sweep through something violently.

quote.citation: 2012, Robin Nicole, For the Sake of Appearances:
quote.text: And so on Friday nights, James Torin tornadoed through six beers, a carton of cigarettes, a coffee table littered with lottery tickets, and unrequited dreams.
They come every night,those cavernous trains, tornadoingthe frozen house,a madness feeling for the door.
